summary: Defines a human-readable text form for LDAP search filters. It replaces RFC 1960 and was replaced by RFCs 4510 and 4515.

plainLanguage.summary: A search filter is a question like "find all the people whose surname is Jensen". This RFC gives that question a written form, so a person and a program can spell the same filter and both be understood.

questions: how to write an ldap filter
how to escape special characters in ldap filter
what does ldap filter ampersand mean
subtitle: A compact, human-readable text notation for LDAP search filters, such as (&(objectClass=Person)(sn=Jensen)).

tldr.problem: LDAP sends search filters over the network in a binary form, but applications and people also want a common way to write a filter as text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a prefix-notation grammar in which each filter sits in parentheses, with & for and, | for or, ! for not, and a backslash-plus-two-hex-digits escape for special characters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2254 replaced RFC 1960 and added LDAP version 3 extended match filters. It has since been replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4515.

facts.label: Notation
facts.value: Prefix; every filter is wrapped in parentheses

facts.label: Logical operators
facts.value: & for and, | for or, ! for not

today: RFC 2254 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4515, and updated by RFC 3377. It replaced RFC 1960.

sections.title: Why a Text Form for Search Filters
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) defines a network representation of a search filter, which is transmitted to an LDAP server. Some applications find it useful to have a common way of representing these search filters in a human-readable form, and this document defines that string format.

It replaces RFC 1960, extending the string LDAP filter definition to include support for LDAP version 3 extended match filters, and including support for representing the full range of possible LDAP search filters.

The document carries an IESG note. LDAP provides both read and update access, update access requires secure authentication, and this document does not mandate implementation of any satisfactory authentication mechanism. Implementors are therefore discouraged from deploying clients or servers that implement the update functionality until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication in LDAPv3 has been published as an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers send questions to a directory server in a binary form. This RFC gives everyone a plain-writing way to say the same question, so that people and programs can share it.

sections.title: The Filter Underneath the Text
sections.content:
An LDAPv3 search filter is defined in Section 4.5.1 of the LDAPv3 specification as a choice of ten forms: and, or, not, equalityMatch, substrings, greaterOrEqual, lessOrEqual, present, approxMatch and extensibleMatch. A substring filter holds a type and a sequence of initial, any and final parts. An attribute value assertion holds an attribute description and an attribute value. A matching rule assertion holds an optional matching rule, an optional type, a match value, and a flag saying whether the attributes of an entry's distinguished name count as part of the entry.

Strings in a filter are limited to the UTF-8 encoding of the ISO 10646 character set. On the wire the filter is encoded using the Basic Encoding Rules, with simplifications described in the LDAP specification. The string form in this RFC is a text spelling of the same structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Underneath, a filter is built from a small set of building blocks, such as and, or, not and equals. The text form gives each block a written symbol.

sections.title: The String Grammar
sections.content:
The string representation is defined by an ABNF grammar and uses prefix notation, so the operator comes first. Every filter is wrapped in parentheses: a filter is "(" filtercomp ")", and a component is an and, or, not or a single item.

  • & followed by one or more filters means and.
  • | followed by one or more filters means or.
  • ! followed by one filter means not.
  • An item compares an attribute with a value using = (equal), ~= (approximate), >= (greater) or <= (less).

An item can also be a presence test written attr=*, a substring match such as attr=initial*any*final, or an extensible match written attr [":dn"] [":" matchingrule] ":=" value, or the same without the attribute name. The RFC notes that although both the substring and present productions can produce the attr=* construct, that construct is used only to denote a presence filter.
sections.plainLanguage: You wrap every test in brackets and put the joining word first. And is an ampersand, or is an upright bar, and not is an exclamation mark.

sections.title: Escaping Special Characters
sections.content:
If a value contains an asterisk (0x2a), an opening parenthesis (0x28), a closing parenthesis (0x29), a backslash (0x5c) or NUL (0x00), the character must be encoded as a backslash followed by the two hexadecimal digits representing its ASCII value. The case of the two hexadecimal digits is not significant.

This simple escaping mechanism eliminates filter-parsing ambiguities and allows any filter that can be represented in LDAP to be represented as a NUL-terminated string. Other characters besides the ones listed above may be escaped the same way, for example non-printing characters. A check for a cn value containing a literal asterisk anywhere in it is written (cn=*\2a*).
sections.plainLanguage: Some symbols already mean something inside a filter, such as the brackets and the star. To use one of them as ordinary text, you write a backslash and a short code for it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives simple filters such as (cn=Babs Jensen), (!(cn=Tim Howes)) and (o=univ*of*mich*). A combined one is (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))), which matches person entries whose surname is Jensen or whose common name starts with "Babs J".

For extensible matching, (sn:dn:2.4.6.8.10:=Barney Rubble) uses matching rule 2.4.6.8.10 and also treats the attributes in an entry's distinguished name as part of the entry. Leaving the attribute off, as in (:dn:2.4.6.8.10:=Dino), applies the rule to any attribute that supports it.

Escaping examples include (o=Parens R Us \28for all your parenthetical needs\29), which writes bracket characters as ordinary text, and (bin=\00\00\00\04), which searches for the four-byte value 0x00000004. Non-ASCII UTF-8 characters can be escaped byte by byte, as in (sn=Lu\c4\8di\c4\87).
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show real questions, such as "find a person called Babs Jensen", and how to write a bracket or a star when you mean it as an ordinary letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the string representation itself has no known security implications. LDAP search filters do, because LDAP servers interpret them to select the entries from which data is retrieved. LDAP servers should therefore take care to protect the data they maintain from unauthorized access.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the question down is harmless. The care is needed by whoever holds the answers: they must not hand private information to just anyone.

viz.caption: THE STRING FILTER GRAMMAR FROM RFC 2254, SECTION 4

data.title: ABNF for string filters
data.code:
filter     = "(" filtercomp ")"
filtercomp = and / or / not / item
and        = "&" filterlist
or         = "|" filterlist
not        = "!" filter
filterlist = 1*filter
item       = simple / present / substring / extensible
simple     = attr filtertype value
filtertype = equal / approx / greater / less
equal      = "="
approx     = "~="
greater    = ">="
less       = "<="
extensible = attr [":dn"] [":" matchingrule] ":=" value
             / [":dn"] ":" matchingrule ":=" value
present    = attr "=*"
substring  = attr "=" [initial] any [final]
initial    = value
any        = "*" *(value "*")
final      = value

viz.caption: EACH WRITTEN FORM AND THE FILTER IT REPRESENTS (RFC 2254)
ESCAPED CHARACTER EXAMPLES FROM RFC 2254, SECTION 5

data.title: Escaping in filters
data.code:
(o=Parens R Us \28for all your parenthetical needs\29)
(cn=*\2A*)
(filename=C:\5cMyFile)
(bin=\00\00\00\04)
(sn=Lu\c4\8di\c4\87)
